# Transformations and Recipes {#sec-recipes}

A recipe records ordered preparation independently of product identity, inputs, contracts, and destinations. DataRaft recipes are not fitted preprocessing models. There is no implicit `prep()` and `bake()` phase.

## A small preparation

```{.r}
preparation <- dataraft.core::dr_recipe() |>
  dataraft.core::dr_step_mutate(premium = round(premium, 2)) |>
  dataraft.core::dr_step_filter(status != "cancelled")

policies <- dr_product("policies") |>
  dataraft.core::dr_add_recipe(preparation)
```

The current recipe API mirrors familiar dplyr verbs: mutate, filter, select, rename, arrange, summarise, and distinct. `dataraft.core::dr_step_transform()` accepts a custom function, formula, or transformation adapter.

## Why record preparation?

An ordinary R function is often enough for one script. A recipe becomes useful when preparation needs to be inspectable, composable, and connected to lineage.

The recipe does not replace dplyr. It records deferred operations so DataRaft can apply them inside a product execution.

## Lookups

`dataraft.core::dr_step_lookup()` adds a checked lookup source. The current implementation reuses relationship checks and can build the lookup as part of the product definition.

```{.r}
brokers <- data.frame(
  broker_id = c(10L, 20L),
  region = c("North", "South")
)

preparation <- dataraft.core::dr_recipe() |>
  dataraft.core::dr_step_lookup(brokers, by = "broker_id", name = "brokers")
```

The output contract should describe the data *after* preparation, including columns added by the lookup.

## Recipes and static column lineage

For a restricted set of mutate, select, and rename operations, `dataraft.core::dr_column_lineage()` can inspect direct field dependencies without executing expressions. Unsupported transformations return `complete = FALSE` rather than guessing.

That conservative behavior is important. Incomplete lineage must never be presented as proof that no dependency exists.

## Keep transformations ordinary when ordinary is enough

Do not wrap every function in a recipe step just to make the architecture look formal. Use a recipe when deferred composition, inspection, or consistent execution adds value. Use a normal R function when the operation is local and self-contained.

## Recipes create a visible preparation boundary

There is nothing wrong with an ordinary R function for a transformation. DataRaft accepts custom transformations because real preparation cannot always be expressed as a small set of dplyr verbs. A recipe becomes useful when you want the sequence itself to be inspectable and composable.

That visible sequence enables several things. The product can describe its preparation without executing it. An IDE can show steps. Static column lineage can reason about a supported subset. Tests can target the recipe independently from storage. The same preparation definition can also be attached to more than one product definition when that is genuinely appropriate.

The tradeoff is that a recipe is not magic. Dynamic selectors, arbitrary functions, external services, and opaque transformations can exceed what static inspection can prove. DataRaft responds conservatively. For example, `dataraft.core::dr_column_lineage()` returns `complete = FALSE` when it cannot establish dependencies rather than inventing a lineage map.

### Lookups make dependencies explicit

A lookup is more than a `left_join()` when the relationship itself is part of the workflow. `dataraft.core::dr_step_lookup()` records the lookup as a named preparation step and uses DataRaft's dependency and relationship checks. Use it when a reference dataset is a meaningful input to the product.

Keep large business joins understandable. If a recipe grows into dozens of transformations with several independently useful outputs, that is often a signal that the workflow contains multiple products rather than one enormous product.

::: {.callout-note title="Under the hood"}
Recipe expressions retain their R environments. This is convenient, but it also means that reproducibility still depends on external bindings you capture. Prefer explicit product sources for business data and stable constants for configuration. A recipe is inspectable preparation, not an isolation sandbox.
:::

## Exercises

1. Create a recipe that rounds a numeric field, renames a column, and then selects the final interface. Inspect the recipe before running a product.
2. Replace one declarative step with an ordinary R function. What do you gain, and what metadata or static understanding might you lose?
3. Choose a transformation in one of your existing scripts and decide whether it belongs inside a reusable recipe or should remain local to a consumer.
